# Summary {.unnumbered}

Anthologies of African American literature agree with one another far more
about *who* belongs than about *which texts* represent them. Two anthologies
from different publishers share, on average, about a quarter of their authors
but only about 7% of their works.^[Mean pairwise Jaccard overlap across the
317 cross-series edition pairs: $J_A = .247$ for authors, $J_W = .068$ for
works, with excerpts coalesced into their parent works (the primary work
unit; dropping excerpts or counting them as distinct works gives the same
qualitative picture). Same-series pairs are excluded from all agreement
statistics in this report.] This report asks what that gap actually means, by
building selection models and testing which of them can predict real
anthologies. Three questions, three answers:

1. **Is the gap just arithmetic?** Partly. With ~600 candidate authors and
   ~3,000 candidate works, almost any selection process agrees more about
   authors than works, so the *direction* of the gap proves nothing — it is
   not "improbable," only counterintuitive for a criticism that locates value
   in texts. For works to out-agree authors, selection would have to be
   *more* author-centered, not less: either each author carries a few
   signature works that every editor converges on (a heavily weighted die),
   or authors receive so many selections apiece that matches pile up (many
   rolls of a fair one). The first is unsupported by the data and the second
   runs against the shrinkage of per-author space documented elsewhere in
   this project.^[Structurally,
   with single-author works and equal per-author allocations, work-level
   Jaccard can never exceed author-level Jaccard under author-first
   selection; inversion requires strong within-author concentration combined
   with large allocations tilted toward commonly shared authors. The real
   edition shapes supply the allocations, but the fitted within-author
   concentration is weak ($\alpha \approx 0.5$) and fails model selection
   below. So A > W is the expected signature of *weakly* author-valuing
   selection — the observed record — while W > A would paradoxically signal
   a canon that values authors more.] What arithmetic does not supply is the
   *magnitude*: no single "shared canon of authors" process reproduces the
   observed pattern of agreement.

2. **Do editors share preferences for authors, for works, or both?** Authors,
   strongly: a model that knows which authors were anthologized before
   predicts later anthologies far better than chance. Works, essentially no —
   once one fact is taken into account: a new edition of an *existing series*
   keeps about three quarters of its predecessor's works, while unrelated
   anthologies re-select fewer than one in five. So work selections are
   highly predictable from the same series' own prior edition and nearly
   unpredictable from *other editors'* prior choices. Modeling that
   self-copying explicitly turns out to explain an order of magnitude more
   than any cross-editor work preference, and once it is in the model, adding
   a work preference makes predictions *worse* in five of six specifications.

3. **Does any simple shared-canon process fully account for the record?** No.
   Even the best model — shared author propensity plus series self-copying —
   still understates how much *independent* editorial teams agree with each
   other, about authors and even about works. Cross-editor work choice is
   therefore not literally random: it is weak, an order of magnitude less
   structured than author choice, and what little structure exists is
   exactly what no tested process explains. That residue is the genuinely
   unexplained (and most interesting) part of the corpus.

The defensible thesis is therefore:

> Anthology selection is organized primarily through authors, and at the work
> level primarily through each series revising itself. Apparent cross-editor
> consensus on particular works is mostly series self-inheritance. The
> agreement that remains among independent editors exceeds every stable-canon
> process tested here and requires historical and institutional explanation.

A corollary worth stating plainly: the only place in this record where a
*particular text's* canonicity is legible is series self-inheritance — that
is, precisely where no fresh editorial judgment occurs. Wherever judgment is
fresh, the name persists and the text is drawn anew.

# The two regimes of reselection

The single most consequential fact for modeling is that "reselection" mixes
two very different behaviors. Editions that continue a series (NAAAL 1997 →
2004 → 2014 → 2025; *Afro-American Writing* 1972 → 1985; *Cavalcade* 1971 →
1991; *African American Literature* 1993 → 1998) are revisions: they inherit
most of their predecessor. Editions from different series are independent
selections:

| Pair type | Pairs | Work retention | Author retention | $J_W$ | $J_A$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Within-series | 8 | 73.9% | 87.5% | .563 | .660 |
| Cross-series | 317 | 18.4% | 51.6% | .068 | .247 |

Any analysis that pools these regimes will mistake series inertia for
cross-editor consensus, in two ways: a "how often was this work selected
before?" score counts a work carried through four NAAAL revisions as four
times more canonical than a work chosen once, and a prediction test whose
later anthologies are mostly series follow-ups rewards a work effect simply
because NAAAL reselects NAAAL. The models below therefore count prior
selections by distinct *series*, and give candidates that appeared in the
focal edition's immediate same-series predecessor their own explicit
carryover effect.^[An earlier draft of this analysis, lacking both controls,
found a "modest but real" cross-series work effect; that finding does not
survive them. A still earlier draft found that a single author-canon
simulation could reproduce the corpus summaries; that fit depended on three
implementation errors (latent works that could never recur across editions,
excerpts silently dropped rather than folded into parents, and candidate
pools seeded by the very anthology being predicted) and disappears when they
are corrected — none of 500 corrected simulations comes as close to the data
as required (joint $p = .002$ in every work-unit specification).]

# How the models are tested

Every model re-selects the 26 anthologies with their observed *shapes* held
fixed — the same number of authors and the same works-per-author allocation
as the real edition — so models differ only in **what drives selection**:

- **Uniform**: any eligible author, any of their works.
- **Author-only**: authors with stronger prior track records are favored;
  works within an author are free.
- **Work-only**: individually favored works drive selection and drag their
  authors in.
- **Mixed**: both effects at once.
- Each of the above **with or without series carryover**: candidates that
  appeared in the edition's same-series predecessor get an extra boost.

That yields eight nested families.^[Formally, for an allocation slot of $k$
works, author $a$, and work subset $S$: $P(a,S \mid k,U) \propto
R_A(a)^{-\gamma}\, e^{\delta_A \mathbb{1}[a \in P_A]}
\binom{|\Omega_a|}{k}^{-1} \prod_{w\in S} R_W(w)^{-\alpha}\,
e^{\delta_W \mathbb{1}[w \in P_W]}$, where $U$ is the set of still-unused
authors, $\Omega_a$ is $a$'s eligible oeuvre, and $P_A, P_W$ are the author
and work sets of the most recent same-series predecessor. Marginalizing over
work subsets lets strong works pull their author in, so work-only is a real
alternative rather than uniform author choice in disguise. Author ranks are
prior AFAM selection counts over distinct series; work ranks use selection
conditional on author inclusion, $q_w = (n_w + 1/2)/(n_{a(w)} + 1)$, on the
same series basis, with midranks for ties. Authorless works get the same
treatment in their own likelihood; coauthored bundles (rare) are excluded and
reported. A latent-oeuvre inflation parameter $\lambda$ allows unobserved
works; it fits to zero, which the likelihood cannot distinguish from
unidentifiability, so oeuvre size remains an open question.]

Validation is chronological, so no model ever peeks at what it predicts.
Parameters are tuned only on anthologies up to a cutoff (1991 or 1998), with
each training edition scored using only strictly earlier records; rankings
are then frozen and the model must predict the *actual selections* of the
anthologies published after the cutoff. The score is the model's log
probability of each real choice — literally, how unsurprised the model is by
what the later editors did.^[Grids: $\gamma, \alpha \in \{0,.5,1,1.5,2,3\}$,
$\lambda \in \{0,1,3,7\}$, $\delta_A, \delta_W \in \{0,2,4,6\}$, chosen by
conditional log predictive density on training editions from 1968 onward. The
carryover deltas are identified by the same-series successors inside each
training window (1985 and 1991, plus 1998 at the later cutoff). Predictions
condition on observed novelty: identities absent from all pre-cutoff records
are outside the frozen pool, and coverage is reported (at the 1998 split the
pool covers 83.0% of held-out author selections and 72.9% of authored-work
selections; at 1991, 67.0% and 41.8%). The carryover indicator for a held-out
edition uses its predecessor's *realized* contents — history available at
prediction time, never the focal outcome.]

Finally, each family's best model must pass a texture check it was never
fitted to: simulate the entire held-out period 400 times and compare the
simulated pattern of pairwise agreement to the observed one.^[Eight reserved
statistics — cross-series $J_A$, $J_W$, the share of pairs agreeing more on
authors than works, the share of shared authors with zero shared works, the
temporal slopes of both Jaccards, and within-series $J_A$ and $J_W$ — are
evaluated jointly with covariance estimated on half the simulations and
calibrated on the other half. Simulated series chain through their own
*simulated* predecessors, so within-series correlation is generated, not
copied in.]

# What the models show

## Authors are the backbone

Knowing which authors have been selected before, and favoring them, is worth
about one log unit per selection decision over uniform choice on held-out
anthologies — roughly an $e$-fold gain in the probability of each real
choice — and it helps on series continuations and on fresh anthologies alike. Pure work-driven selection performs *worse* than uniform. This
is the strongest and most stable effect in the corpus short of series
carryover itself.

## Work-level agreement is series self-copying

Held-out log score per selection decision, primary specification (higher is
better; **bold** = best per cutoff):^[Coalesced work unit. "Chained" columns
in the output CSVs split these totals into editions with and without a
same-series predecessor; the carryover gain is concentrated entirely in the
chained editions (3.5–4.9 log units per decision), as it should be.]

| Family | 1998 cutoff | 1991 cutoff |
|---|---:|---:|
| Uniform | -10.74 | -9.19 |
| Author-only | -9.64 | -8.20 |
| Work-only | -10.98 | -9.34 |
| Mixed | -9.42 | -8.05 |
| Series-only | -7.36 | -7.58 |
| Author+series | **-6.51** | -6.81 |
| Work+series | -7.74 | -7.68 |
| Mixed+series | -6.65 | **-6.77** |

Two things stand out. First, *every* family with series carryover beats
*every* family without it — even bare self-copying with no author or work
preferences at all (series-only) out-predicts the best canon-style model.
Adding carryover to the author-only model improves the held-out total by
1,188–2,017 log-score units depending on specification; the cross-series work
effect an earlier draft reported was worth about 120–140.

Second, once carryover is in the model, the work preference stops earning its
keep: adding it changes the held-out total by $-95$ at the 1998 cutoff and
$+32$ at 1991 — the latter being the only specification, out of six (three
work units × two cutoffs), where any cross-series work effect survives model
selection, and by a trivial margin.^[Margins per decision, best vs.
runner-up: drop $+.244$ and $+.158$, include $+.274$ and $+.108$, coalesce
$+.147$, all favoring author+series; coalesce/1991 favors mixed+series by
$+.035$. One honest residue: on *fresh* editions at matched $\gamma$, a small
work term still improves the coalesced score by $\approx .2$ per decision at
both cutoffs, so a weak cross-editor work preference on series-opening
anthologies remains possible — but it is specification-sensitive and joint
selection rejects it five times out of six.] The earlier "modest work
effect" was series inertia wearing a work-canon costume.

## What no model explains

All 48 model–specification combinations fail the reserved texture check (all
at the calibration floor, $p = .005$). The failure is informative. For the
primary 1998 analysis, observed agreement vs. the best model's simulations:

| Reserved statistic | Observed | Author+series simulates |
|---|---:|---:|
| $J_A$ between independent editions | .475 | .330 |
| $J_W$ between independent editions | .156 | .043 |
| $J_A$ within series | .876 | .686 |
| $J_W$ within series | .732 | .593 |

Carryover recovers most of the within-series texture that canon-style models
miss entirely (they simulate within-series $J_W$ of .163 against an observed
.732). What no family reproduces is how much *independent* editorial teams
agree — on authors and, notably, on works. A stable popularity ranking plus
series self-copying is not enough; the missing structure plausibly includes
period and form coverage requirements, direct influence between anthologies,
changing curricula, and editor or publisher lineages, none of which are
identifiable from only 26 editions.

# Caveats

- The database records anthology appearances, not publication dates or
  complete oeuvres, so "eligible" means "seen in an earlier anthology" and
  predictions are conditional on previously represented identities.
- The held-out periods are small (six editions after 1998, eleven after
  1991); scores are descriptive comparisons, not population estimates.
- Carryover models only the immediate same-series predecessor, with one
  strength shared by all series, learned from the two or three same-series
  successors available before each cutoff.
- The texture failures show the model space is incomplete; they do not say
  which omitted mechanism is responsible.

# Reproducing {.unnumbered}

```bash
# focused methodological regression tests
uv run pytest -q \
  tests/test_author_work_agreement_models.py \
  tests/test_author_work_agreement_stress.py \
  tests/test_author_work_agreement_bundle.py

# corrected author-canon grid (repeat for --work-unit drop / include)
uv run python analysis/overlap/author_work_agreement_models.py \
  --mode fit --work-unit coalesce --phantom-scope shared \
  --fit-trials 100 --save-csv \
  --out-fit output/author_work_agreement_models_fit_coalesced_shared.png \
  --out-fit-csv data/author_work_agreement_models_fit_coalesced_shared.csv

# full prequential grids (gamma, alpha, lambda, delta_A, delta_W),
# both cutoffs, 400-trial
# held-out checks; series-basis ranks and carryover are the defaults
# (--rank-basis editions / --deltas 0 restore the legacy model)
uv run python analysis/overlap/author_work_agreement_stress_test.py --save-csv
```

Principal outputs: `data/author_work_agreement_stress_{train_grid,holdout,
ppc,coverage,series_gap}.csv`, plus
`data/author_work_agreement_corrected_best500.csv` and
`data/author_work_agreement_eligibility_leakage.csv`.
